title: BAPTISM, BELOVEDNESS, WILDERNESS: NOTICE THE ORDER IN JESUS’ STORY
paragraphs: BAPTISM, BELOVEDNESS, WILDERNESS: NOTICE THE ORDER IN JESUS’ STORY

Before Jesus faced the devil in the wilderness, the Father spoke over the Son at the Jordan. Before the temptation came the declaration. Before the battle came belovedness. And if you reverse that order in your own heart, you may spend your entire Christian life trying to earn what can only be received through Christ.
There is an order in the story of Jesus that exhausted Christians desperately need to notice.
Jordan.
Beloved.
Wilderness.
Not wilderness first.
Not victory first.
Not “prove Yourself first.”
Jesus comes up from the water, heaven opens, the Spirit descends, and the Father speaks.
Then the wilderness comes.
That order matters.
Because some of us have quietly rewritten Christianity into something Jesus never taught.
We tell ourselves:
Fight hard enough, and maybe God will love you.
Become holy enough, and maybe God will want you.
Stop struggling, and maybe God will accept you.
Serve more.
Pray longer.
Read another chapter.
Break the addiction.
Fix the marriage.
Control the thoughts.
Clean up the secret.
Become useful.
Become impressive.
Become spiritual.
And then...
perhaps...
God will finally look at you and say,
“Now I am pleased with you.”
But look again at Jesus.
Matthew records that after Jesus was baptized, He came up from the water, the heavens opened, and the Spirit of God descended like a dove upon Him. Then came the voice:
“This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”
In Greek:
Οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ υἱός μου ὁ ἀγαπητός, ἐν ᾧ εὐδόκησα.
Houtos estin ho huios mou ho agapētos, en hō eudokēsa.
“This is My Son, the beloved, in whom I delighted / was well pleased.”
That word ἀγαπητός — agapētos carries the sense of one who is beloved, dearly loved, precious.
And we must be careful here.

Jesus is not merely an insecure human being receiving a motivational speech about His self-esteem. He is the eternal Son of God. The baptism of Jesus reveals something infinitely greater than a technique for feeling better about ourselves. The Father speaks concerning His Son, the Spirit descends upon Him, and Jesus enters His public messianic ministry.
The scene is gloriously Trinitarian.
Father.
Son.
Holy Spirit.
And the Father's declaration also resonates with the Scriptures Israel already knew.
Psalm 2 speaks of God's royal Son:
“You are my Son...”
Isaiah 42 introduces the Servant whom God upholds, His chosen one in whom His soul delights, upon whom He puts His Spirit.
At the Jordan, these biblical currents converge upon Jesus.
The King.
The Servant.
The beloved Son.
The Messiah.
And then Matthew writes something we might rush past:
Τότε ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἀνήχθη... εἰς τὴν ἔρημον
“Then Jesus was led... into the wilderness.”
Then.
Do not miss that word.
The wilderness did not interrupt the story.
It was the next scene.
Jesus went from the Father's public declaration into a place of hunger, isolation, testing, and confrontation.
And the tempter came.
Notice how the temptation begins:
“If You are the Son of God...”
Do you hear it?
At the Jordan:
“This is My beloved Son.”
In the wilderness:
“If You are the Son of God...”
The Father declares.
The tempter challenges.
And suddenly this ancient scene begins feeling painfully familiar.
Because the enemy still loves attacking what God has spoken.
God says He is merciful.
Your shame whispers, “Not to someone like you.”
Scripture says there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
Your past whispers, “Except for what you did.”
Christ says His sheep hear His voice and He gives them eternal life.
Fear whispers, “You will be abandoned eventually.”
The Gospel announces grace.
Your wounds whisper, “Earn it.”
Maybe that is where you are right now.
You love Jesus...
but you're tired.
You believe the Gospel...
but somewhere underneath your theology is a terrified little courtroom where you keep putting yourself on trial.
Every failure becomes evidence.
Every unanswered prayer feels like rejection.
Every dry season feels like abandonment.
Every temptation makes you question whether your faith was ever real.
Every time somebody else seems more blessed, more disciplined, more successful, more joyful, more “used by God,” something inside you asks:
“What is wrong with me?”
And then you start performing.
Not because obedience is wrong.
Obedience is beautiful.
Jesus Himself says that those who love Him keep His commandments.
But there is a catastrophic difference between obeying God because you are trying to purchase His grace and obeying God because His grace has already found you in Christ.
One is slavery to spiritual performance.
The other is the fruit of salvation.
Christianity is not:
Perform → become worthy → earn grace → become God's child.
The Gospel announces something radically different.
We are sinners who cannot save ourselves.
Christ came for sinners.
Christ died for sinners.
Christ rose from the dead.
And those who repent and believe are reconciled to God through Him.
Paul writes:
Τῇ γὰρ χάριτί ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι διὰ πίστεως...
“For by grace you have been saved through faith...”
And then:
“...not a result of works, so that no one may boast.”
Ephesians 2 does not leave us lying on the floor doing nothing, however.
Immediately afterward comes the beautiful reversal:
“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works...”
Grace does not eliminate obedience.
Grace puts obedience in its proper place.
Good works are not the price of salvation.
They are the fruit of salvation.
You do not obey Jesus so that His blood will become sufficient.
You obey because His blood is sufficient.
You do not repent so you can impress God with how sorry you are.
You repent because the kindness of God leads you to repentance.
You do not fight sin to convince Jesus to become your Savior.
You fight sin because Jesus is a Savior worth following.
And perhaps someone reading this has spent years reversing the order.
Wilderness.
Performance.
Exhaustion.
Failure.
Shame.
Try again.
Hide.
Pretend.
Smile at church.
Say, “I'm blessed.”
Go home.
Collapse.
Repeat.
But Jesus' story confronts our obsession with proving ourselves.
At the Jordan, before the wilderness temptation, the Father's declaration concerning His Son has already sounded.
Then Satan essentially invites Jesus to prove Himself.
“If You are the Son of God, command these stones to become bread.”
Jesus is hungry.
Really hungry.
Forty days.
And He certainly possesses divine authority.
Yet He refuses to let the devil dictate the terms on which His Sonship must be demonstrated.
He answers with Scripture.
“Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.”
That comes from Deuteronomy 8, where Israel's wilderness experience is in view.
Israel had been called God's son.
Israel passed through water.
Israel entered wilderness.
Israel was tested.
And Israel failed repeatedly.
Jesus enters the waters.
Jesus enters the wilderness.
Jesus is tested.
And where Israel failed, the faithful Son obeys.
Where Adam fell amid abundance, Christ remains faithful amid hunger.
This is why we cannot reduce Jesus to merely our inspirational example.
We need more than an example.
We need a Savior.
If Christianity were simply, “Look how perfectly Jesus lived; now go do the same,” we would still be doomed.
We cannot climb our way to God by imitation.
The scandal of grace is that the One who did not sin came to rescue sinners who did.
The beloved Son walked toward a cross.
And there, the One who heard the Father's declaration at the Jordan would hear mockers weaponize strangely familiar words:
“If You are the Son of God, come down from the cross.”
Again...
“If You are...”
Prove it.
Use power for Yourself.
Escape suffering.
But Jesus stayed.
He stayed.
Not because nails were stronger than Him.
Not because Rome had defeated Him.
Not because He lacked authority.
Jesus said no one took His life from Him; He laid it down willingly.
The beloved Son went willingly toward the place of shame so that rebels could be reconciled to God.
That is the Gospel.
And this is where the story stops being comfortable.
Because you cannot stare at the cross for very long while continuing to pretend your sin is harmless.
Grace is free to us.
It was not cheap.
Our forgiveness has blood on it.
Our redemption bears scars.
The cross tells you simultaneously that your sin is worse than your excuses admit...
and God's grace in Christ is greater than your shame dares believe.
Maybe your wilderness has a name.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Secret messages.
Alcohol.
Pride.
Envy.
Greed.
A marriage growing cold.
A child who no longer calls.
A prayer that seems unanswered.
A diagnosis that changed the atmosphere of your home.
A church wound you still carry.
A private habit nobody knows exists.
Or maybe nothing dramatic happened.
Maybe you simply became tired.
You used to pray because you wanted God.
Now you pray because you feel guilty when you don't.
You used to open Scripture hungry.
Now three verses feel heavy.
You still worship...
but sometimes the words leave your mouth before they reach your heart.
And somewhere along the way you started believing that wilderness means God has rejected you.
But look at Jesus.
The wilderness came immediately after the Jordan.
Difficulty is not, by itself, evidence of divine abandonment.
In Jesus' case, Matthew explicitly says He was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil.
That does not mean every hardship in our lives has the same purpose or that God tempts people to evil. James explicitly says God tempts no one.
It means something simpler and more powerful:
You cannot measure God's faithfulness merely by the comfort of your circumstances.
Sometimes faithfulness looks like bread multiplied.
Sometimes faithfulness looks like trusting God's Word while your stomach is empty.
Sometimes faithfulness looks like Lazarus walking out of a grave.
Sometimes faithfulness looks like Stephen seeing heaven opened while stones are falling.
Sometimes God changes the circumstances.
Sometimes He sustains His people through them.
But the center of Christian confidence is never the ease of the wilderness.
It is Christ.
And here we need another careful distinction.
Jesus' unique Sonship is not identical to ours.
He is the eternal Son by nature.
Believers become children of God through Him—by grace, through faith, through adoption.
John says of Christ:
“To all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God.”
Paul writes that in Christ we receive adoption.
So Christians do not stand before God saying, “I deserve what Jesus deserves.”
We stand amazed saying:
“I belong to Jesus.”
That changes everything.
Because if your confidence ultimately rests upon your spiritual performance, every wilderness will destroy your peace.
One terrible week and you'll think God left.
One relapse and you'll think grace expired.
One season of doubt and you'll assume Jesus has changed.
But if your hope rests upon Christ...
you can confess without pretending.
You can repent without bargaining.
You can crawl back after falling.
You can say, “Jesus, I sinned,” without adding, “so now I must hide from You.”
That is what shame wants.
Hide.
Grace says come into the light.
Shame says cover yourself.
Grace points to Christ.
Shame says prove you are worth rescuing.
The Gospel says the Rescuer already came.
Perhaps the most dangerous Christian is not the believer who knows he is weak.
It may be the believer who has become skilled at looking strong.
Some of us have learned Christian camouflage.
We know when to raise our hands.
We know which verse to post.
We know how to say “God is good” while quietly bleeding.
We know how to answer, “How are you?”
“Blessed.”
But heaven is not impressed by our costumes.
Jesus did not die for the person you pretend to be.
He died for sinners.
Real ones.
People with histories.
People with scars.
People who failed after promising never again.
People who discovered that knowing the right verse does not automatically silence every temptation.
People who have cried in bathrooms so nobody would hear.
People who worship on Sunday and wrestle on Monday.
People like Peter, who swore loyalty and then denied Jesus.
Peter's failure became public.
His restoration became personal.
“Do you love Me?”
Jesus did not pretend Peter's denial never happened.
Grace does not rewrite history by calling evil good.
Jesus rewrites the future by redeeming people who cannot undo yesterday.
That is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior:
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because repentance becomes unnecessary.
Not because holiness no longer matters.
But because your worst chapter does not possess more authority than the crucified and risen Christ.
The cross is stronger than your scandal.
The empty tomb is stronger than your past.
And repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is the mercy of God calling you out of the grave you were decorating like a home.
So stop trying to turn stones into bread just to prove who you are.
Stop making every achievement testify in your defense.
Stop demanding that your career prove you matter.
Stop demanding that your marriage prove you are lovable.
Stop demanding that your ministry prove you are anointed.
Stop demanding that applause prove you are significant.
Stop demanding that your suffering disappear before you believe God is faithful.
Look to Christ.
Because eventually every human voice goes quiet.
Followers disappear.
Bodies age.
Money moves.
People misunderstand.
Success evaporates.
And the wilderness asks the question we spend our lives avoiding:
When everything you used to prove yourself is stripped away...
is Jesus enough?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Not because a comment saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing the struggle into the light is the first crack in the wall we've spent years building around ourselves.
Somebody scrolling silently tonight may need to know that Christians can struggle deeply without Christ abandoning His people.
Not as an algorithm trick.
Not because forwarding a Facebook article earns favor with God.
It does not.
Send it privately to the person whose smile has not convinced you.
God's grace cannot be purchased.

But if Gospel Warrior is helping you know Christ, understand Scripture, repent honestly, endure your wilderness, and bring biblical truth to people who desperately need it, supporting this work can be one practical way of helping that work continue.
If you want to glorify God through your support, let the motive be love for Christ and love for people—not fear, guilt, or an attempt to buy blessing.
Jesus is.
Stay close.
Because eventually another wilderness will come.
And when it does, you may need to remember the order.
Jordan.
Beloved Son.
Wilderness.
Temptation.
Obedience.
Cross.
Resurrection.
And for those who belong to Christ, the wilderness does not get to write the final sentence.
Maybe you arrived here believing you had to become impressive enough for God.
Maybe you've been dragging chains that Jesus has been calling you to confess.
Maybe your scandal is still fresh.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody knows.
Either way, do not run from Christ.
Run to Him.
Repent.
Believe.
Come into the light.
There is forgiveness in Jesus.
There is mercy in Jesus.
There is restoration in Jesus.
There is no Savior hiding behind the Savior.
Jesus Himself is the refuge.
And when the wilderness whispers, “Prove yourself,” remember where salvation rests.
Not in your flawless record.
His.
Not in your blood.
His.
Not in your resurrection.
His.
Not in your ability to hold onto God with perfect strength...
but in the Christ who saves His people.
So when you fall, repent.
When you hurt, pray.
When you doubt, bring the doubt to Christ.
When temptation comes, answer with truth.
When shame tells you to hide, step into the light.
When the wilderness feels endless, remember that Satan did not write Jesus' ending.
The grave did not write Jesus' ending.
Rome did not write Jesus' ending.
The crowd did not write Jesus' ending.
And because the risen Christ is Lord, your sin does not have to write yours.
And comment before you leave.
Not something polished.
Something true.
“Jesus, I surrender.”
Or simply:
“Pray for me.”
Because perhaps the person who needs to stop hiding today...
is you.
And remember this when the wilderness becomes loud:
The voice of temptation may question what God has spoken, but it cannot rewrite who Jesus is—and your wilderness can never become more powerful than your Savior.
